extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of aesthetics, psychology, and the theory of humor (general educated readers interested in humor theory)
extracted.subtask_description: A survey of theoretical accounts and empirical observations about what produces laughter and comic response (derision/superiority, play, disappointment/incongruity, Bergson's mechanism, tickling studies, and related qualifications). Useful for analysing or producing humorous material grounded in psychological/aesthetic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derision / Superiority Theory (Hobbes, Descartes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arises from a feeling of superiority, derision, or 'secret elation and pride of heart' when we perceive some inferior quality or misfortune in another; Descartes: 'Derision or mockery is a kind of joy mixed with hate...' .
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original accounts emphasize scorn/hatred mixed with joy. The textbook records many criticisms and softenings of this view (e.g., the necessity to limit derision to slight/inconsequential misfortunes, or to interpret it playfully). Empirical evidence (Lillien J. Martin) shows not everyone reports a feeling of superiority when amused. Use this criterion when analysing humor that explicitly hinges on contempt or triumphant scorn; beware that it does not account for playful or affirmative laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeising's three-phase comic process
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic involves (1) a shock from an object that seems to be something but is not, (2) a counter-shock of enlightenment in which we recognize the object's nothingness, and (3) a 'happy sense of superiority to that nothingness' which causes laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation refines derision theory by making surprise and recognition stages explicit. Apply when analysing jokes that depend on an initial deceptive appearance followed by revelation and a resulting sense of elevation; highlights temporal structure (setup → reveal → reaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Groos' inward imitation / aesthetic participation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the second phase of Zeising's process there may be a moment of 'inward imitation' of the absurdity; aesthetic perception involves transporting oneself into the object between shock and enlightenment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that comic perception can be aesthetic: partaking in the absurdity before distancing oneself. Use when humour depends on playful identification with the ridiculous (e.g., humorous role-play, benign mimicry). Suggests that too much derisive distance reduces the aesthetic/participatory quality of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful derision / 'fighting-play' (Ziegler, Groos)
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh at the stupidities and misfortunes of others only when they are slight and inconsequential and our scorn is essentially playful; Groos terms this 'fighting-play.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualifies superiority accounts: for humor to be acceptable or playful, the target's misfortune must be slight; the mood is one of sport rather than malicious Schadenfreude. Use this as a normative criterion for 'benign' humor and to distinguish cruel jokes from playful teasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature or object-as-derider (Schiitze) / Comic Spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative view attributes the deriding mood not to the laugher but to the object/nature that brings intended sublimities to a fall — we enjoy perceiving that 'she is playing a game.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames comic effect as perception of a natural irony or the world overturning our pretensions. Apply when humour arises from situational irony or the environment exposing human limits rather than a subject's active scorn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schauer's teasing / joy-of-play account; objective vs subjective comic
rubrics_metrics.description: All comic enterprise is identified with teasing: 'Teasing is a game in which the players take the role of adversaries...' Schauer divides comic experience into objective-comic (jokes in which we triumph) and subjective-comic (jokes in which we are triumphed over).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recasts many comic situations as playful contest rather than egoistic hostility. Useful to analyse reciprocal teasing, jokes that alternately put us in the role of victor or victim, and to emphasize the game-like structure of many comic interactions. Note caution in the textbook: must free theory from assumption of egoistic hostility to reach full 'joy of play' insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play-attitude as prerequisite for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'play-attitude' (a particular pleasurable mood or nervous-system condition) is often necessary for humor: tickling and other playful provocations succeed only when the subject's mind 'welcomes fun' and is not alarmed, ill, or preoccupied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observations (Sully, Darwin, tickling studies) show mood/state is decisive: serious, alarmed, or preoccupied subjects will not respond with laughter even to the same stimulus. For producing humor, ensure audience is receptive (playful mood); for analysis, treat audience state as a moderating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disappointment / Incongruity Theory (Kant, Schopenhauer, Dumont)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arises from a 'sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing' (Kant) or from perceiving an incongruity between a concept and the real object subsumed under it (Schopenhauer): unexpected subsumption/mistake produces the ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the classic incongruity account: set up an expectation (concept) and then reveal a perceptual or factual contradiction. The text records strengths (explains surprise-based jokes) and limits (too intellectualist, does not cover all quick, reflexive laughter). Useful for analyzing witticisms, punchlines, and many cognitive jokes; beware that affective or purely sensory humour may not fit neatly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schopenhauer's perception-victory account and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Schopenhauer: laughter comes from the victory of perception over abstract thought — perception (concrete, immediate, satisfying) displaces the inadequate abstractions of thought; this intellectualist account reduces many jokes to a 'syllogism' form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains pleasure in being 'proved' right by perception, but the textbook criticizes its exclusivity: many laughs are reflexive, musical, bodily, or not intellectual. Use when humor depends on conceptual misclassification or 'paradox,' but do not treat it as universally explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bergson's mechanistic vs. living contrast; laughter as corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh at 'the rigid, the ready-made, the mechanical ... automatism in contrast with free activity.' Laughter carries an 'unavowed intention to humiliate, and consequently to correct' — it is on the side of life and intelligence, incompatible with sympathy-driven emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly applicable to satire and caricature: humor highlights mechanical, habitual, or inelastic behavior and functions as a social corrective. The text notes Bergson's theory is more about the art of satire than all forms of laughter, and that it may exclude cases where sympathy/pity or pure play produce laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tickling mechanics (Dumont's empirical observations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tickling produces laughter when there are unexpected variations in speed, direction, or interval of touches; no laughter when touches are uniform or self-administered. Observations summarized: (1) uniform stroke = no laughter; (2) equal successive touches at equal intervals = no laughter; (3) unexpected changes of direction/interval = laughter; (4) varying rapidity/direction can cause laughter even without interruption; (5) one cannot tickle oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete conditions support the idea that unexpectedness/variation (not mere sensation) triggers laughter in tickling. Use as a model for physical-play humor: introduce unpredictable variation and avoid fully predictable patterns; ensure stimulus is not self-generated by the eventual laugher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical modifiers: individual differences, novelty/familiarity decay
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical studies (Lillien J. Martin; H. L. Hollingsworth) show individual variation (not all subjects report superiority), that 'unexpectedness' and 'contrast' are commonly present in comedic stimuli, and that jokes wane as they become familiar — different jokes decay at different rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating humor account for audience heterogeneity and the rapid loss of comic effect with anticipation/familiarity. Hollingsworth's curves indicate some jokes retain value longer than others; novelty and the inability to quickly anticipate the punchline are important evaluative dimensions.
